Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 356 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2019) 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 356 is a forested unit including boreal central mixedwood and foothills natural 
subregions. The unit is located west of the Forestry Truck Road, covering an area of 6526 km2. Industrial activity 
has been high throughout this unit over the past 20 years. Oil and gas development and exploration, gr avel 
extraction and forest harvest have resulted in a large network of roads throughout WMU 356. Currently there is an 
early (September 24 to October 31) and a late (November 1 to November 30) antlered moose special licence 
season, and an antlered moose archery-only, non-draw licence season (August 25 to September 23) within this 
WMU.  
A survey for moose was last conducted in 2014 using distance sampling methods. In 2014 the moose population 
was estimated to have 2755 individuals (90% CI 2204 - 3443), a density of 0.42 moose/km2, and a bull:cow:calf 
ratio of 31:100:26 (Table 1). The goal of this survey was to assess the status of moose since the last survey in 
2014. Specific objectives were to determine a population estimate, population ratio for sex and age classes and a 
density estimate for moose in WMU 356. 
Survey Method 
An aerial survey for moose in WMU 356 was conducted from February 11 to 13, 2019. Distance sampling methods 
(Buckland et al., 2001) were used to determine moose population and density estimates. Distance sampling 
transects (n = 363), up to 10 kilometres in length and oriented north-south, were established throughout the unit 
with 1.8 kilometre spacing. A random sample of 100 transects was flown for a total survey effort of 891 kilometres. 
Moose were classified by age (adult or calf) and sex. Other wildlife observations were also recorded. 
 
Results 
Two hundred and thirty-six moose were observed in 159 independent groups. Of the 236 moose observed, 233 
individuals were successfully classified:  
 
 Fifty-seven (25%) were bulls 
 129 (55%) were cows 
 47 (20%) were calves 
 
Of the bulls observed, 79% had already shed their antlers. Of the bulls still with antlers, three-quarters were small 
(small spike or forked antlers), and one-quarter were medium (small palmated antler ‘paddles’). No large bulls 
(large palmated antlers with minimum 3 points to the front with a spread more than half the body length) were 
observed. The bull:cow and calf:cow ratios were 0.44 and 0.36, respectively. The density estimate was 0.61 
moose/km2 with a coefficient of variation of 13%. The estimated moose population for WMU 356 is 3970 (90% CI 
3216 - 4900).  
 
We also observed 10 white-tailed deer (1 fawn, 1 doe and 8 unclassified), 1 unclassified mule deer, 41 elk (21 
cows, 6 bulls, 2 calves and 12 unclassified) and 1 coyote, however these should not be considered minimum total 
counts as this survey method is unreliable for these species in heavily forested units or where populations are at 
low density.
